steps.observation: Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every evening at dusk, Thomas wound the mechanism by hand.

He had done it for thirty-one years — the creak of the gears, the smell of the lamp oil, the slow bloom of light that pushed out across the black water. He knew the rhythm of it better than his own heartbeat.

The island was small enough to walk across in ten minutes. There was a cottage, a garden where nothing much wanted to grow, and the tower. That was the whole of Thomas's world, and he had made his peace with it long ago.

Ships still passed, though fewer than before. He logged them in his ledger each morning — names, times, directions. Some nights he could hear the low groan of a foghorn answering his light, and he felt, in those moments, like he was having a conversation.

In October, a young inspector came from the mainland with a clipboard and soft shoes. He walked around the tower twice, nodded, and told Thomas that the light would be automated by spring. A computer would do it. There would be no need for a keeper.

Thomas poured the man tea and said nothing.

After the inspector left, he climbed the tower stairs as he always did. He wound the mechanism. The light turned.

Somewhere beyond the dark horizon, he imagined a sailor looking up from the wheel of some tired vessel, seeing the beam sweep across the water, and feeling — without quite knowing why — that everything was going to be all right.

Thomas figured a computer could probably manage the light just fine.

But he wondered who would stay up worrying about the ships.
